old_title: Iran war live: Iranian cyberattacks 'targeted critical US infrastructure'
new_title: Iran war live: Vance says 'things happen' after US accused of wedding strike
old_text:
Iranian hackers have targeted critical American infrastructure with cyberattacks in recent weeks, a new report has claimed, as fresh strikes threatened to plunge Washington and Tehran back into all our war.
Four sources with access to government and industry information about cyberthreats told NBC News that hackers are believed to have targeted US telecommunications, energy and other infrastructure, bringing the war ever closer to the American public.
The attempts have focused on automated systems connected to the internet but have not been successful so far, according to the report, noting that new threats against energy, water and telecommunications were still emerging on Telegram over the weekend.
The FBI said at the end of July that at least seven states have been targeted in a growing wave of cyberattacks on critical water infrastructure across the country. Officials were said to be investigating Iran as the likely agent behind the attacks, per PBS.
The latest threats emerged as the US and Iran exchanged attacks across the Middle East, with US forces striking Iran's southern coast and Iran firing at American bases across the region.
The United States threatened more devastating strikes. Iran accused Washington of hitting a wedding party, killing five people and wounding dozens.
In pictures: Damage after alleged US strike on Iranian wedding kills five
The latest: Trump aides 'desperately trying to stop war escalating' despite renewed strikes
Donald Trump's top White House aides are urgently pushing to prevent the Iran war from escalating, after the US ramped up the intensity of its attacks on Wednesday.
The aides want to prevent the war escalating before November's midterm elections to stem Republican electoral losses, four sources told the Reuters news agency.
Officials will consider once again ramping up military action after the vote in November, but a return to the full-scale conflict is not a given, they said.
"We are keeping the pressure on Iran," one White House official said. "But November is a priority."
Saudi Arabia says Iranian attack killed two seafarers in Strait of Hormuz
As we reported earlier, Saudi Arabian shipping company Bahri reported that two Filipino seafarers had been killed in a security incident in the Strait of Hormuz.
Saudi Arabia, the world's biggest crude exporter, has now confirmed that an Iranian attack on an oil tanker owned by its national shipping company killed the seafarers.
Sidr, owned by Bahri, was one of two supertankers carrying Saudi oil reported to have been hit late on Monday while transiting the Strait of Hormuz.
Tehran has threatened tankers attempting to sail through the narrow waterway without authorisation, impeding energy exports from neighbouring oil-rich Gulf countries.
About one-fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas trade used to pass through the Strait of Hormuz before the US and Israel launched strikes on Iran on February 28.
"The kingdom stressed the necessity of halting escalations, and respecting international maritime safety and the security of global energy supplies," the Saudi foreign ministry said.
"Bahri remains in continuous contact with the vessel and is coordinating closely with the relevant authorities and maritime industry stakeholders, while continuing to closely monitor developments," the company said in a statement.
US Centcom says it 'never targets civilians' after wedding strike
US Central Command has denied targeting civilians after Iranian media reported at least four people were killed in a US strike on a wedding in Sirik, southern Iran.
"The US military never targets civilians, unlike the Revolutionary Guards," CENTCOM told the Reuters news agency on Wednesday.
Iranian people are victims of Tehran's decisions, says France's UN ambassador
Iranian people are the victims of the decisions made by Tehran's authorities, France's UN ambassador and September's president of the Security Council Jérôme Bonnafont has said.
"They are the victims of the choices made by the Iranian authorities for years now, with these episodes of mass repression," he told reporters according to Iran International.
"At the heart of our discussions on Iran this month will be the nuclear issue," Bonnafont added.
The council is set to discuss the sanctions committee tired to Iran's nuclear programme this month.
"We will look at the noncompliance of Iran with its nuclear obligations and the consequences arising therefrom."
Bonnafone added that the disruption in the Strait of Hormuz was having "extremely adverse" consequences.
Car hits pro-government gathering in Iran, killing four
A car struck a gathering of supporters of Iran's government and armed forces in the northeastern city of Mashhad overnight, killing four people and injuring more than 10, several Iranian media reported on Wednesday.
A car travelling at high speed first collided with another vehicle, lost control and then veered into the crowd after hitting safety barriers and traffic signs, Noor News reported, citing Mohsen Mousa-Abadi, head of Razavi Khorasan Province's traffic police.
Initial checks showed the driver, who was arrested, was not in a normal state, Mousa-Abadi said, without giving details on his condition.
There was no immediate indication of a political motive, and authorities described the incident as a traffic accident.
The evening gathering was one of a series of recurring events attended by supporters of the Islamic Republic and its armed forces since the war with the United States began in late February, according to Mehr news agency.
Watch: US Central Command releases video showing wave of strikes on Iranian military targets
The latest: Trump has no interest in 'worthless' deal with Iran as both sides launch new strikes
US president Donald Trump has insisted he "couldn't care less" if Iran signs a "worthless" deal to end the war, as both sides launched fresh strikes in the spiralling conflict.
The conflict in the Middle East saw a dramatic re-escalation on Wednesday as Washington and Tehran traded attacks in the biggest exchange of fire in weeks, with US forces attacking Iran's southern coast and Iran attacking American bases across the region.
"I'm not trying to force Iran to the bargaining table," the Trump wrote on Truth Social overnight, responding to speculation after the US struck Iran for the first time since July overnight into Monday. "I couldn't care less if they sign a worthless, to them, agreement."
How Iran could stop more even oil leaving the Middle East
Mohsen Rezaei, the former Revolutionary Guards chief and secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, has threatened to shut down oil exports.
He has warned the US that if the economic war continues, not a single drop of oil will be exported through the Strait of Hormuz or anywhere in the Persian Gulf.,
Iranian attacks and threats to shipping have already stopped most traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, largely shutting down a waterway that carried around a fifth of global energy before the conflict.
Although some oil tankers have been moving through the strait in recent weeks, volumes remain very low.
Missile, drone or speedboat attacks on tankers trying to leave the Gulf have repeatedly pushed up oil prices during the six months of the conflict.
Meanwhile, Tehran's Houthi allies have restricted Red Sea shipping with attacks and threats to blockade all Saudi Arabian shipping, which carries crude to Asia through the Bab el-Mandeb strait past the group's Yemeni stronghold.
While the attacks initially only stopped some vessels, with more than half still getting through in mid-August, the situation is difficult for shippers with Chinese shipping companies now rerouting away from Bab el-Mandeb, according to industry sources.
Further attacks, such as the one that targeted a vessel off the main Saudi Red Sea oil terminal at Yanbu last week or a drone strike near the Suez Canal in early August, could raise oil market anxiety levels and crude oil prices.
With Reuters
new_text:
JD Vance has faced backlash after appearing to dismiss reports that a US strike killed five people, including two children, at a wedding gathering in southern Iran.
When asked about whether a US strike was responsible, he said "sometimes things happen".
He said: "I will say that the Iranian state media has not been a very good scribe about what's happened in the conflict thus far, so I'm extremely sceptical of this."
The toll was confirmed not by the Iranian government but by the Iranian Red Crescent, a member of the International Red Cross and Red Crescent Movement.
"What I can say with 100% confidence is that, unlike the [Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps] IRGC, the United States never targets civilians in combat," Vance said. "We never will do that. We never have done that, and unfortunately, obviously, sometimes things happen."
Meanwhile, president Donald Trump insisted he had done the "right thing" with the war.
It comes amid fears Trump is planning to extend Washington's war on Iran, after The Wall Street Journal reported that the Pentagon was extending the presence of troops in the Middle East into next year.
Araghchi defends Iran over strikes on Jordan
Iranian foreign minister Abbas Araghchi takes to social media to respond to his Jordanian counterpart's recent comments criticising Iran for strikes on Jordan and neighbouring countries.
The Jordanian minister Ayman Safadi said that attacks on his country came within two hours of the start of the war, in February, suggesting the attack was not reactionary.
Araghchi writes: "How much time does the Jordanian Foreign Minister believe Iran should wait before responding to an aggressor that respects neither Arab sovereignty nor Iranian sovereignty?"
He adds: "And is he truly unaware that Arab airspace, lands, and waters were used in the initial American attacks that resulted in the killing of innocent Iranians?"
Evidence points to US weapon in deadly strike on Iran wedding celebration
The United States is investigating a deadly strike on a wedding gathering in southern Iran after weapons experts reviewing verified images and video concluded the blast was likely caused by a direct hit from a U.S. munition, Vice President JD Vance said Thursday.
Five people have died following Tuesday's strike on a home hosting the celebration, according to Iranian state television, which reported Thursday that a 22-year-old woman had died from her injuries. Iranian officials said nearly 70 others were wounded.
Speaking to reporters Thursday, Vance confirmed U.S. authorities were examining what happened.
"We're investigating it because obviously we care. We want to know," Vance said.
Trump claims US has 'unlimited' munitions amid Iran war concerns
Donald Trump has denied persistent reports that the Iran war has dangerously depleted the U.S. weapons stockpile, blasting the media for what he claimed was false reporting on the state of the American arsenal.
"For the treasonous SCUM that refuses to accurately report on our Military Operation in Iran, we have virtually unlimited amounts of Mid to High Grade Ammunition, far more than we could ever use for this, or for any other War (which is highly unlikely!), that could improbably take place," he wrote Thursday on Truth Social.
"In addition, we are producing Munitions at levels never seen before," he added. "We are stockpiling and preparing for any contingency that could happen."
In focus: Sailors on USS Abraham Lincoln describe 'the worst deployment'
US service members assigned to the USS Abraham Lincoln are speaking out about their record-long, nearly nine-month deployment at sea, during which they supported the ongoing Iran war.
The Nimitz-class aircraft carrier - some of whose crew had reportedly suffered from deteriorating mental health - laid anchor off Thailand this week, affording its 5,000 sailors and Marines their first port call in 286 days.
While on shore in the resort town of Pattaya, some service members spoke with MS NOW Pentagon Correspondent Priya Sridhar, who recounted her discussions with them during a subsequent on-camera interview.

Watch: White House launches arcade games based on Trump's agenda
This morning: Asian benchmarks mostly rise after tech stocks lead rally on Wall Street
Asian shares were mostly higher in early Friday trading, as regional market sentiment got a boost from the rally on Wall Street, mostly from big technology stocks.
Japan's benchmark Nikkei 225 rose 0.6% in morning trading to 64,622.33. South Korea's Kospi gained 0.9% to 6,635.67. Australia's S&P/ASX 200 was little changed, slipping less than 0.1% to 9,011.80. Hong Kong's Hang Seng jumped 2.1% to 25,751.26, while the Shanghai Composite added 0.8% to 3,973.27.
Stocks on Wall Street closed higher Thursday as a recent run-up in bond yields eased further and big technology companies rallied. The S&P 500 rose 1.1%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 1.2%, and the Nasdaq composite closed 1.4% higher.
The latest:
Shipping traffic through Hormuz well below normal, Kpler data says
Shipping traffic through the Strait of Hormuz remained well below normal on Thursday, with only four commodity vessels crossing the key waterway, according to preliminary Kpler data cited by Reuters.
That was down from nine crossings the day before and well below the 10-day average of about 15.
The vessels included two medium-range tankers, a Kamsarmax tanker and a Handysize vessel.
Vance refuses to give a deadline to end US war on Iran
JD Vance has declined to give a timeline for ending the US war on Iran, while downplaying the conflict by saying there was no active shooting and major combat had lasted only about six weeks.
"I wouldn't call it a war. Right now, there is no active shooting," Vance said. He added: "I recognise there have been places where this has flared up."
"When you ask, 'When will this end?', you're asking me a question like: When will the Iranians stop shooting at ships?" Vance told reporters.
"I think the reality is, I don't know the answer to that question. You'd have to ask the Iranians."
His remarks come after days of intense fighting between the US and Iran.
Israel says economic pressure on Iran could push the regime to take 'desperate steps'
Israel's defence minister has warned that growing economic pressure could push Tehran to take more desperate measures.
"We see signs indicating that the heavy economic pressure they are under, and the fear of an uprising and the collapse of the regime, may push them to desperate steps," Israel Katz said.
Earlier, Iran had claimed that it had the capability to manufacture more missile stockpiles and maintained enough in its war against the US"Initially, some believed that Iran had only a limited number of missiles and that its stockpiles would eventually be depleted as the war continued," the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps spokesperson Brig Gen Hossein Mohebbi said.
"However, that assumption proved incorrect, as Iran's missile capability has remained sustained and its missile production has continued."
Trump rejects reports of US weapons stockpiles running low
Donald Trump has rejected reports that US military stockpiles of weapons are running dangerously low as the war with Iran enters its seventh month.
In a post on his Truth Social platform he wrote that the US was producing munitions at "levels never seen before" and has "far more than we could ever use".
"For the treasonous SCUM that refuses to accurately report on our Military Operation in Iran, we have virtually unlimited amounts of Mid to High Grade Ammunition, far more than we could ever use for this, or for any other War (which is highly unlikely!), that could improbably take place," Trump wrote.
"In addition, we are producing Munitions at levels never seen before. We are stockpiling and preparing for any contingency that could happen. We are taking them for ourselves, the U.S.A., rather than selling them to others, but the sales to Allies will soon again, begin. Also, please let it be known, that the Biden Administration gave far more Munitions away to Ukraine, at no cost to them, whatsoever, than we have used in Iran."
